doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: High school music course, arranging, and Ernie Washington and other pianists
summary: He drops auto mechanics for music, tries writing arrangements, and describes Ernie Washington, John Dennis and Ray Bryant at Little Falls.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Exactly. One word. Fallbackon. Something like alpaca. But I listened to her and took auto mechanics for about 2-1/2 years in high school, totally wasting my time. I’m horrible in mathematics and you need to know geometry and stuff to be — you have to have machinist skills to be a really good auto mechanic and so forth. And I was a 98 pound weakling and couldn’t loosen the bolts on engine heads and all that. And then finally I realized well this is a waste of my time. I love cars but I’m not good at it. I’m good at music. I’m a teenager and I’m playing with grown-ups, and they’re telling me I’m good. So I switched to a music course I think in my senior year, or late junior year, had to sort of go back and start all over again.
Was it at UFA? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

At Proctor. Ronnie Zito went to UFA. We were best friends and it was like being on opposite sides of the country at that time as a teenager. But I started the music courses, took Rudiments of Music and History of Music and so forth. The rudiments teaches you key signatures and so forth, before theory where you learn harmony and all that. And I got this bug that I wanted to write some arrangements, like Gerry Mulligan’s quartet with no piano. And I did, just by sort in my head solfeggio. And somehow I got some guys in my high school who played in the orchestra to come to my house and try to play the arrangements. And they didn’t have a clue. It sounded pretty horrible. The notes were all right but their phrasing, they didn’t have a clue. They weren’t interested in jazz, and they weren’t really talented they just happened to play instruments. And then I don’t know, somehow I got hooked up with Ronnie and Torrie Zito and I went to their house and brought my arrangements and they played them and I said, “That’s the best?” That was my last foray into writing. But I guess that sort of was like my entree into meeting Sal Amico and Vic Kirch. J.R. was always living in New York and Ernie Washington, and Gordon Smith and these other guys. Ernie Washington was truly a great artist, a great pianist who had some of the greatest facility. He could play as fast as anybody I ever heard, and he played trumpet too as a hobby, but when he played trumpet he sounded to me like Idrees Sulieman, the big fat sound and it sounded like he blew hard. Curiously enough his embouchure was over here not in the middle. But he had a piano studio in New Haven near Yale and taught privately and I think he was from Philadelphia. And he grew up with those older guys, the Heath brothers, and he once told me that the first place Charlie Parker ever stayed in New York was at Ernie’s apartment here in New York. And that’s really a shame that he didn’t get well documented. He was a friend of Ray Bryant and John Dennis. John Cowth Dennis, who died young but who was a contemporary of Ray Bryant. He was also from Philly, John Dennis. And there was a small place in Little Falls called The Corner Tavern and a friend who had a car drove me there a couple of times and said, “You can’t believe some of the pianists they’re bringing in here, just guys doing a single.” And the two guys I saw were Ray Bryant and John Dennis. It was just astounding.
Wow, in Little Falls, New York.
